# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- California became a U.S. state in **1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely.
- An estimated **300,000 people** arrived from across the US and abroad during the Gold Rush, producing a transient, predominantly male, and ethnically diverse population.
- The defining event is the January 1848 gold discovery at Sutter's Mill, sparking mass migration.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **California, County Births, 1850–1919** (FamilySearch collection 2017276, ~789,456 people) — county-level, indexed on FamilySearch, covers the target period.
- **California, County Marriages, 1850–1952** (FamilySearch collection 1452832, ~1,135,780 people) — county-level, overlapping the Gold Rush window.
- **California, Mission Records, 1769–1850** (FamilySearch collection 1804372, ~98,765 people) — baptisms, marriages, and burials through 1850; useful for Californio families already settled before the Rush.
- ⚠️ The FamilySearch Wiki's California-specific vital records pages could not be fully loaded during this survey, so precise civil-registration start dates at the state or county level remain unconfirmed here.

### Census Records
- A **California State Census, 1850–1852** digitized volume exists (image group 006601001, 522 images, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable).
- The **1850 federal census** is the first to enumerate California as a state.

### Land & Mining Claim Records
- A **Mining Claim Registers** volume for San Francisco, 1849–1855 was found (image group 006601002, 340 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**) — you must page through images manually.
- For Spanish/Mexican-era land grants predating the Rush, the BLM General Land Office (GLO) site is the standard online source, though California-specific coverage was not confirmed by tool results in this survey.
- Federal land patents for public-domain mining parcels (post-1850) are also available at the BLM GLO site.

### Arrival / Immigration Records
- A **Port Arrival Registers** volume for Sacramento, 1849–1858 was found (image group 006601003, 298 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**). Note that many Gold Rush arrivals came through the **Port of San Francisco** — no equivalent San Francisco arrivals volume was returned in this survey; that is a gap to investigate.
- NARA holds federal passenger lists for Pacific-coast ports; full manifests list all family members, including children.

### Voter / Residency Records
- **California, Great Registers, 1866–1910** (FamilySearch collection 1923340, ~1,345,678 people) starts just after this window (1866), but is useful for confirming a migrant's continued presence in California into the 1860s.

### Records With Known Tool Limitations
- Probate, court, church, newspaper, and tax records for this period were **not confirmed as digitized** in this survey. The FamilySearch catalog search returned zero hits — a tool-coverage gap, not proof these records are absent. Physical custodians (county courthouses, California State Archives in Sacramento) hold them.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds for This Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County Births/Marriages, Mission Records, State Census, Mining Claim Registers (browse-only), Port Arrival Registers (browse-only), Great Registers from 1866 | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census, general vital records | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Passenger lists, naturalizations, federal land patents | Free / by request |
| **BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov)** | Federal land patents | Free |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Gold Rush–era newspapers, obituaries | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service/pension records | Subscription |
| **California State Archives (Sacramento)** | Probate, court, and land records (physical holdings) | In person / by request |

---

## Records Not Online
- **Mining claim registers** and **port arrival registers** are digitized but not indexed — browse-only images only.
- Probate, court, and most county-courthouse land records were not confirmed as digitized in this survey.

---

## Known Hazards
- The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire is widely known to have destroyed many city and county records. No tool result in this survey confirmed specific Gold Rush–era losses from that event, so verify directly with the relevant repository before concluding a record is gone.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's California-specific pages (vital records, land and property, census, naming conventions) returned only generic content during this survey — re-fetching those pages directly before relying on this guide's absence of detail is recommended.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Identify the specific county or mining camp** first. The county birth, marriage, and land record series are filed at the county level; a statewide search will only go so far.
2. **Check Mission Records** for anyone already in California before 1848 (Californio families, Spanish/Mexican-era settlers).
3. **Budget time for manual image browsing** — mining claim registers and port arrival registers require paging through hundreds of unindexed images.
4. **Examine full passenger manifests**, not just the head of household — spouses, children, and traveling companions are listed too.
5. **Great Registers (from 1866)** can confirm whether your ancestor remained in California after the Rush ended, even though they fall outside the 1848–1860 window.
6. **Volume_search returned 14 digitized volumes** for California 1848–1860, but only 3 were examined in this pass — additional browseable volumes may exist and are worth checking on FamilySearch directly.

---

*This guide covers California statewide for 1848–1860. For deeper results, narrow to a specific county (e.g., El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Sacramento) and run a follow-up search at the county level for vital, probate, and land records specific to that mining district.*

# Locality Guide: New York City, 1700s Colonial Period

Here is what the research found for tracing families in colonial-era New York City (1700–1800):

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

New York City was under British colonial rule during most of this period (1664–1783), then transitioned to U.S. state jurisdiction after the Revolution. The city had an active Dutch-descended population alongside English, French, and other settlers. Major denominations included Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian churches, all of which kept records.

---

## Key Record Types & FamilySearch Collections

| Record Type | Collection / Notes | FamilySearch ID |
|---|---|---|
| **Church Records** | New York, Church Records, 1640–1940 (~2.3M persons) | 1469062 |
| **Land Records** | New York, Land Records, 1630–1975 (~1.6M persons) | 2078654 |
| **Probate Records** | New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971 (~988K persons) | 1542780 |
| **Tax Records** | New York, Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799–1804 | 1678432 |

**Digitized Browse Volume Found:**
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City, 1700–1776** — image group **007733180**, 211 images. This is in Dutch, **not name-indexed**, and must be browsed page by page.

---

## Important Gaps

- **No civil vital registration** was confirmed for this period — church registers are the primary substitute for births, marriages, and deaths.
- **No census records** apply; the first U.S. federal census was 1790. Tax rolls (starting 1799) are the nearest substitute.
- **No court records, immigration/naturalization records, or colonial military collections** were found digitized for this place and period.
- Anglican and Presbyterian church registers were not confirmed as separate digitized collections, despite both denominations being active in the city.
- Pre-1799 tax rolls were not found in this survey.

---

## Repository Tips

- **FamilySearch.org** (free) — start with the four collections listed above. The Church Records collection (1640–1940) is the most important entry point for the colonial period.
- **New York State Archives** and the **NYC Municipal Archives** typically hold original colonial-era land, court, and probate records, but their specific colonial-era holdings could not be confirmed from tool results in this survey.
- **Ancestry.com** (subscription) — worth checking for New York colonial-era holdings, particularly church transcriptions and land records.
- **Fold3** (subscription) — for any colonial/Revolutionary War military records.

---

## Practical Advice

1. Because no civil registration existed, **church records are your foundation**. Identify your ancestor's denomination first.
2. The confirmed colonial church register on FamilySearch (Dutch Reformed, 1700–1776) is **browse-only and in Dutch** — plan to work through it image by image and use translation help for Dutch entries.
3. **Land and probate records** often name family members and neighbors; these are especially valuable when vital records are absent.
4. **Search the statewide collections** on FamilySearch — the Land, Church, and Probate collections span the whole state and may include New York City entries not broken out separately.

---

No boundary-change data was returned by the tools for New York City itself across 1700–1800; the city's administrative status shifted from Dutch colonial (pre-1664) to English/British colonial (1664–1783) to U.S. state jurisdiction (post-1783/1788), but this survey could not confirm finer jurisdictional detail from the FamilySearch Wiki (see gap below).

No port-of-entry or naturalization collection specific to this place/period was returned. New York City was the Province's principal port, so such records likely exist but were not surfaced by this survey.

`collections_search` lists **"New York, County Marriages, 1847-1849; 1907-1936"** (id 1920153) — entirely **outside** the 1700s target window; not useful for this research period.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies and the most militarily prolific — it contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony.
- The war's climactic battle (Yorktown, 1781) was fought on Virginia soil.
- County-level record-keeping in Virginia dates to the 1630s.
- Note: Virginia's western territory during this period included Kentucky County (formed 1776, became the state of Kentucky in 1792); families near the frontier may need a separate locality guide.

---

## Available Record Types

### Military Records
Per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Virginia Military Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War):
- **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — National Archives, Record Group 93
- **Virginia militia records** — held at the **Library of Virginia**, Richmond
- **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files** — National Archives, Record Group 15
- **Virginia State Navy records** — published and available separately
- **FamilySearch digitized collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (collection id 1945678, ~345,678 persons) — date range exactly matches the war

**Research tip:** Check pension and bounty-land files (NARA RG 15) even if no service record survives — many veterans appear only in the pension series.

---

### Land Records (Including Post-War Bounty Lands)
- Virginia granted bounty lands to veterans in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio**; warrant and survey records linking veterans to their land claims are held at the **Virginia State Library**.
- **Digitized browse volume:** "Revolutionary War land bounty warrants," Virginia, 1779–1800 (image group 005301447, 341 images, 0% name-indexed — must be browsed image by image).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection id 1734285, ~2,567,890 persons)

**Research tip:** If an ancestor's Virginia service is suspected but their later residence is unknown, search the Military District of Ohio warrant/survey records — bounty land often relocated veterans out of Virginia entirely.

---

### Census Substitutes (Tax Lists)
- **The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms 1780s county tax lists as the standard substitute.
- **Digitized volume:** "State enumerations / tax lists," Virginia, 1782–1799 (image group 005301449, 87 images, full-text searchable, 0% name-indexed)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection id 1456723, ~456,789 persons)

---

### Church Records
- The established Anglican (Church of England) parish was the primary pre-registration vital record keeper during this era.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (collection id 1598230, ~1,234,567 persons)
- Originals are held in parish/diocesan archives.

---

### Probate and County Court Records
- Wills, inventories, administrations, and guardianships were recorded at the county court level.
- **Digitized volume found:** "County court order books," Augusta, Virginia, 1775–1795 (image group 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-searchable — browse remaining 39%)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (collection id 2134567, ~1,789,012 persons)

---

### Cemetery Records
- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) — curated external link for Virginia burials

### Newspaper Records
- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) — wartime notices, casualty reports, estate/legal notices

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | What It Covers | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Military 1775–1783; Land/Marriage/Will 1600–1900; Church 1680–1929; Tax 1782–1850; County Court 1650–1920 | Free |
| **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) | Dedicated military records, including Revolutionary War files | Subscription |
| **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/) | Continental Line muster rolls (RG 93); pension/bounty-land application files (RG 15) | Free (in-person or online request) |
| Find A Grave | Burial locations | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia** (Richmond) | Virginia militia records |
| **Virginia State Library** | Bounty-land warrant and survey records |
| County courthouses | Original court order books, deeds, probate |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Continental Line records; pension/bounty-land application files |

---

## Known Record Losses
- **1790 Virginia federal census** — destroyed (British burning of Washington, 1814). **Substitute:** 1780s county tax lists.

---

## Summary & Next Steps

Virginia's Revolutionary War research is well-supported by records at the National Archives (service and pension files), the Library of Virginia (militia records), and the Virginia State Library (bounty-land warrants). Because the 1790 census is lost, 1780s tax lists are your primary census substitute for locating families at war's end.

To narrow the search, let me know the **specific family name and county** you're tracing — that will point us to the right county courthouse, parish, and bounty-land record set.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts — 1840s Port Immigration

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

Boston was a major Atlantic seaport and commercial center. The 1840s saw a massive influx of Irish immigrants fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852); by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born. Boston sits within Suffolk County, Massachusetts (statehood 1788), and no significant boundary changes affect the city for this period.

---

## Key Record Types & Where to Find Them

### 🚢 Passenger Lists (Immigration)

- **FamilySearch — "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891"** (collection id 1784312, ~1.23 million people) — the primary name-indexed collection for port arrivals.
- **FamilySearch — Port of Boston Passenger Lists, 1840–1850** (image group 003345210, 389 images) — digitized but only **3% name-indexed**; use **full-text search** rather than name-index browsing. This volume is the most direct source for arrivals in your window.
- **NARA (National Archives)** — holds the original customs passenger lists; accessible in person or by written request.

> ⚠️ Because the 1840–1850 volume is barely indexed by name, search by approximate date, ship name, or origin port when a name search fails.

---

### 📜 Naturalization Records

- **FamilySearch — "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906"** (collection id 1459213, ~345,678 people)
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — state, county, or federal — not necessarily near where the family settled. Search broadly, not just Suffolk County.

---

### ⛪ Church Records

- **FamilySearch — "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (collection id 1921657, ~987,654 people)
- Catholic parishes expanded rapidly in the 1840s to serve Irish immigrants. Parish sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often pre-date or supplement civil registration.
- Specific Boston parish names were not confirmed by tool results in this survey; the **Archdiocese of Boston archive** (written request) holds original parish registers.

---

### 📋 Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **FamilySearch — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (collection id 2061550, ~3.46 million people) — covers 1840s Boston at the town level.
- For events before civil registration was well established, use church records as an alternative.

---

### 📰 Newspaper Records

- ***The Pilot*** (Boston Irish Catholic newspaper) published **arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements** placed by families trying to reconnect with newly arrived immigrants — a unique and often overlooked source.
- Check Boston-area newspaper archives and **Newspapers.com** for this period.

---

### 🗂️ Census Records

- The **1840** and **1850 U.S. federal censuses** bracket this period. The 1850 census was the first to name every household member individually — extremely useful for newly arrived immigrant families.

---

## Repository Quick Reference

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger lists, naturalization, church, vital records (all collections above) | Free |
| NARA | Original customs passenger lists, naturalization case files | In person / written request |
| Archdiocese of Boston archive | Parish sacramental registers | Written request |
| Suffolk County courthouse | Court & naturalization records | In person / mail |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers incl. *The Pilot* | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |

---

## Records Gaps & Cautions

- The FamilySearch catalog returned **zero hits** for "passenger lists" at Boston/Suffolk — treat this as a cataloging gap, not proof the records are absent; the NARA series is not confirmed as fully online.
- Specific 1840s Boston Catholic parish registers are **not confirmed as online** in this survey; the diocesan archive is the best avenue.
- No tool result confirmed a specific record-loss event for Boston 1840s immigration records.

---

## Recommended First Steps

1. Search **FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891"** (id 1784312) by surname.
2. Run a **full-text search** on the 1840–1850 Port of Boston volume (003345210) for the surname, variant spellings, and approximate arrival years.
3. Follow up in the **Massachusetts Naturalization Records** collection for the same individuals.
4. Check **Massachusetts Town Vital Records** and **Massachusetts Church Records** for post-arrival baptisms, marriages, and deaths.
5. Search ***The Pilot*** newspaper for arrival or missing-persons notices.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States (1840s — Port Immigration Focus)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston is a long-established city (FamilySearch dates its standard place from 1630); Suffolk County is its enclosing county.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts (statehood 1788)
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for this call — could not confirm 1840s figures through this tool.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport and commercial/shipping center.
- **Ethnic composition:** Per Wikipedia, large-scale Irish immigration in the 1840s (Great Famine era, 1845–1852); by 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes grew rapidly to serve the Irish immigrant influx (not independently confirmed by a tool result here — see gap below).
- **Key historical events:** Great Famine-driven Irish immigration surge, 1845–1852 (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
No boundary changes affecting Boston/Suffolk County were returned by these tools for this period; treat Boston/Suffolk as stable for 1840s research.

## Available record types

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of Boston (the specific focus of this request).
- **Record types / what exists:** `volume_search` found one digitized volume covering exactly this window: image group 003345210, "Passenger Lists, Port of Boston," 1840–1850, 389 images, only 3% name-indexed but **full-text searchable** — so it is reachable via full-text search even though a name-index browse will mostly fail. `collections_search` separately lists "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection id 1784312, ~1.23 million people) at FamilySearch, which overlaps the 1840s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized); original customs passenger lists are a National Archives (NARA) record series for U.S. ports.
- **Access:** Use the "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" collection for name search first; for the specific 1840-1850 Port of Boston volume (003345210), use full-text search rather than name-index browsing, since only 3% is indexed by name.
- **Content note:** Examine full manifests — infants and children traveling with parents are listed alongside adults, so check every name on a given sheet, not just the head of household.

### Naturalization records
- **Types:** Declarations of intention and naturalization petitions; pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (state, county, or federal), not necessarily where the immigrant later lived.
- **Where held:** `collections_search` lists "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection id 1459213, ~345,678 people) at FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** `catalog_search` for "passenger lists" at Boston/Suffolk returned zero catalog hits — this is a cataloguing gap in what this survey could confirm, not evidence the records don't exist; check NARA directly and FamilySearch's broader Massachusetts naturalization collection.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes serving the Irish immigrant community (per Wikipedia context); specific parish names were not returned by any tool in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — valuable since many new immigrants' events were recorded by the parish before or alongside any civil record.
- **Where held:** `collections_search` lists "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection id 1921657, ~987,654 people) at FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** No tool result named a specific Boston-area parish or confirmed which parish served a given neighborhood — this survey could not pin that down; do not assume a specific parish without further source-level confirmation.
- **Language:** Not stated by any tool result returned here.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No FamilySearch Wiki page specific to Massachusetts vital records start dates could be fetched in this survey (see gap note below) — the generic content returned does not state a Massachusetts-specific date, so I am not supplying one from memory.
- **What exists:** `collections_search` lists "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection id 2061550, ~3.46 million people), which covers the 1840s at the town level.
- **Where held:** Town-level vital records (per that collection's title); access via FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** Specific 1840s Boston gaps not confirmed by these tools.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (above).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1840 and 1850 U.S. federal censuses bracket this period (1850 was the first to name every household member individually). No Massachusetts-specific state census confirmed for the 1840s by tool results here.
- **Access:** Not independently verified for Boston in this survey beyond the collections above; the Ancestry federal census collection link below is a general starting point.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Wikipedia names *The Pilot*, an Irish Catholic newspaper that published arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements for Irish immigrants in this era — potentially valuable for tracing arrivals this survey's record tools don't otherwise index by name.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by a tool result in this survey; worth checking Boston-area newspaper archives and the Catholic diocesan archive.
- **Content value:** Arrival notices, missing-persons ads specifically aimed at reconnecting immigrant families.

### Other record types
Not separately surveyed in this pass; land, probate, military, tax, and cemetery records exist generically for Massachusetts/Suffolk County but were not the focus of tool results returned here.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (id 1784312); Port of Boston passenger-list volume 003345210 (1840-1850, full-text searchable, 3% name-indexed) | Port arrival records | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906 (id 1459213) | Naturalization/citizenship records | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (id 1921657) | Pre-civil-registration vital events | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (id 2061550) | Town-level civil vital records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census enumerations | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives and Records Administration (https://www.archives.gov/) | Original passenger-list and naturalization source records | Free (in person/request) |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military service records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Arrival/missing-persons notices | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` for Migration/Emigration/Naturalization record-type groups returned exactly 1 matching digitized volume for 1840-1850 Boston, and `summary.complete: true` — this appears to be the full matched set for that specific filter, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives (NARA, Boston or Washington) | Original customs passenger lists, naturalization case files | In-person / written request |
| Suffolk County courthouse | Court and naturalization records that may include pre-1906 petitions | In-person / mail |
| Catholic diocesan archive (Archdiocese of Boston) | Parish sacramental registers — specific parish not confirmed by this survey | Written request |

## Records NOT online
- `catalog_search` returned zero hits for "passenger lists" at Boston/Suffolk in the FamilySearch Catalog — treat this as a cataloguing gap for this survey, not proof such records are absent; the full NARA passenger-list and naturalization series for this period are not confirmed as online in full.
- Specific parish-level Catholic sacramental registers for 1840s Boston were not located online by any tool call here.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that any specific Boston 1840s immigration record series was destroyed or lost. I'm not asserting a loss without a source for it.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages this survey tried to fetch (Massachusetts getting-started, online-records, and research-tips pages, plus a Massachusetts Immigration page found by search) all returned only generic placeholder content rather than Massachusetts-specific text — treat this as a gap in what this survey could confirm from the Wiki, not as the Wiki actually saying these things about Massachusetts specifically.
- Because the 1840-1850 Port of Boston passenger-list volume is only 3% name-indexed, rely on its full-text search capability rather than a name-index search, and be prepared to browse/full-text-search by approximate date and ship if a name search fails.
- Check *The Pilot* newspaper (per Wikipedia) for arrival and missing-persons notices, since these can surface immigrants not well captured in indexed passenger-list data.
- Since pre-1906 naturalization could occur in any court of record, do not limit a naturalization search to Suffolk County alone — check state and federal court holdings broadly.

---
Boston was a major gateway for immigrants arriving in the 1840s, especially Irish families escaping the famine years, and the records that can show when and how your ancestors arrived are mainly ship passenger lists kept by U.S. customs (now largely held by the National Archives, with a digitized Boston volume from 1840-1850 available through FamilySearch), plus naturalization paperwork, church baptism and marriage records from the Catholic parishes that served immigrant neighborhoods, and even old newspaper notices placed by families trying to reconnect with relatives who had just arrived. A few cautions worth keeping in mind: the main digitized passenger-list volume for this period is only lightly searchable by name, so it often takes a different kind of search (by date or ship) or old-fashioned browsing; naturalization paperwork from this era could be filed in almost any local court, not necessarily the one near where the family eventually settled; and several of the usual background reference pages this survey tried to check came back without place-specific detail, so some claims above rely mainly on general historical sources and the record collections actually found, rather than a confirmed official guide.

Next, the recommended step is to search the FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" collection and the full-text search on the 1840-1850 Port of Boston volume for the specific family surname, then move to the naturalization and church-record collections named above.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Oklahoma / Indian Territory (mid-1800s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Present-day Oklahoma was designated "Indian Territory" under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. Because Oklahoma was not a state until 1907 — and not even an organized U.S. territory with county government in the mid-1800s — there was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths. Records are organized by **tribal nation and federal agency**, not by county.

The Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) are the central population for this period.

---

## Key Record Types

### Tribal Rolls & Treaty Records *(primary record class)*
- **FamilySearch collection: "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (collection id 1987432, ~568k persons) — directly covers the mid-1800s and is indexed.
- **Digitized Tribal Enrollment Cards** — a volume of ~940 images (image group 002298871, date range 1840–1870, English) found on FamilySearch; 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.
- **Treaty-era annuity payment rolls** — generated by the federal government to administer tribal payments and membership; original records held at NARA.
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — the well-known final enrollment for the Five Civilized Tribes, held at NARA; *postdates* the mid-1800s but useful as a later cross-reference to link back to earlier family lines.

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch collection: "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (collection id 1541872, ~235k persons) — spans the mid-1800s.
- Note: Land in Indian Territory during this period was tribally/communally held under treaty terms — individual allotment came later under the Dawes Act era. These are not standard General Land Office patents.

### Mission/Church Records
- **FamilySearch collection: "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (collection id 1654321, ~123k persons) — includes baptisms, marriages, and burials from missionaries working among the tribes in the mid-1800s.

### Federal Census
No federal decennial census systematically covered Indian Territory residents by name in the mid-1800s the way it did organized states. The **tribal rolls above substitute for census enumeration** of this population in this period.

---

## Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Oklahoma Indian Censuses & Rolls; Early Land Records; Mission & Church Records; digitized Tribal Enrollment Cards (indexed, 1840–1870) | Free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Original tribal enrollment, annuity payment, and treaty records; Dawes Rolls | archives.gov |
| **Tribal Nation Archives** | Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, Chickasaw Nation, Muscogee/Creek Nation, Seminole Nation archives hold their own records | Varies by tribe |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search by tribe/agency, not by county.** No county government existed in Indian Territory in the mid-1800s — always identify the tribal nation first.
2. **The Dawes Rolls are a later record (1898–1914).** They are valuable for confirming tribal membership and linking backward into earlier family lines, but they are not themselves a mid-1800s source.
3. **Treaty-era annuity rolls and mission church registers** are the two record classes most likely to name individuals by name in this period; both are represented in the FamilySearch collections cited above.
4. **Search the FamilySearch Catalog by tribe name** (e.g., "Cherokee Nation") rather than by "Oklahoma" to surface additional catalog materials.
5. **The FamilySearch Wiki's Oklahoma-specific research pages** returned only generic placeholder content during this survey — consult the live wiki pages directly for jurisdiction-specific how-to guidance.

---

This guide covers what confirmed tool results returned. A research plan can be built from here to sequence searches across the tribal rolls, land records, and mission records identified above.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma / Indian Territory, United States (mid-1800s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Present-day Oklahoma was designated "Indian Territory" under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, used for forced relocation of tribes beginning in the 1830s (per Wikipedia); Oklahoma was not organized as a U.S. state until 1907 — `place_search` confirms the FamilySearch standard place "Oklahoma, United States" carries a date range of 1907 onward, meaning no state-level jurisdiction existed in the mid-1800s.
- **Parent jurisdiction (mid-1800s):** Federally administered Indian Territory, not a state or organized territory with county government.
- **Key groups:** The Five Civilized Tribes — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — relocated via the Trail of Tears (Wikipedia, "Oklahoma").
- **Key historical mechanism:** Federal Indian agencies kept annuity rolls, treaty enrollment lists, and agency correspondence rather than civil vital registration.
- **Population/FamilySearch place data:** `place_population` returned no data for "Oklahoma, United States" for 1840–1880 — this survey could not confirm period population figures.

## Boundary changes
Oklahoma had no civil county structure in the mid-1800s; it was unorganized Indian Territory under federal agency administration until the Oklahoma Organic Act (1890) and statehood (1907). Records from this era are filed under tribal/agency jurisdiction (e.g., Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation), not under any county — a researcher must search by tribe and agency, not by modern Oklahoma county.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
No civil registration existed in Indian Territory in the mid-1800s — there was no state or county government to require it. The FamilySearch Wiki page requested for this place returned only generic placeholder content, not Oklahoma-specific detail, so this survey cannot confirm a registration start date; none is asserted here.

### Tribal rolls and treaty records (primary record class for this inquiry)
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection id 1987432, personCount 567,890, dateRange 1851-1959) — this directly covers the mid-1800s window and is indexed.
- **Digitized volume confirmed:** `volume_search` found one digitized, 99% name-indexed and full-text-searchable volume of "Tribal Enrollment Cards" (image group 002298871, 940 images, dateRange 1840-1870, English) covering Indian Territory — indexed + images, reachable by name search.
- **Treaty context:** Treaties (e.g., removal and annuity treaties) generated annuity payment rolls and enrollment lists used to administer tribal membership and land allotment; the later Dawes Rolls (1898-1914, per Wikipedia) are the best-known final enrollment record for the Five Civilized Tribes but postdate the mid-1800s window — useful as a later cross-reference, not a primary mid-1800s source.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration maintains the original tribal enrollment and annuity records (per Wikipedia's note on the Dawes Rolls); FamilySearch holds the digitized/indexed volume above.

### Land records
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection id 1541872, personCount 234,567) — spans the mid-1800s.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land in Indian Territory in this period was tribal/communally held under treaty terms, not distributed via the standard federal rectangular-survey General Land Office patent process used elsewhere — individual allotment did not begin until the later Dawes Act era. This survey's tools did not return a page confirming further detail on the land-distribution office; treat this as unconfirmed beyond the collection cited.

### Church records (mission records)
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection id 1654321, personCount 123,456) — spans the mid-1800s and includes mission-era baptisms/marriages/burials kept by missionaries working among the tribes.
- **Gaps:** This survey could not confirm which specific denominations or mission stations are covered, or any gap years, because the FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched for this place returned only generic placeholder content rather than Oklahoma-specific detail.

### Census records
No federal decennial census covered Indian Territory residents by name in the mid-1800s in the way it did organized states/territories; the tribal rolls above substitute for census enumeration of this population in this period. This survey found no state/territorial census collection for Oklahoma in the tool results.

### Probate, court, and military records
`catalog_search` for "Oklahoma, United States" returned zero hits (`totalHits: 0`) — a cataloging gap in this survey, not evidence these records don't exist. Report this plainly: probate, court, and military records affecting Indian Territory residents in this period (e.g., federal agency court matters, later Civil War-era service by tribal members) were not surfaced by this search and would need a targeted catalog search by tribe/agency name.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (id 1987432); "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (id 1541872); "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (id 1654321); digitized Tribal Enrollment Cards volume (image group 002298871) | Tribal enrollment/rolls, land, and mission records for the period; the digitized Tribal Enrollment Cards volume is name-indexed and full-text searchable | Free |
| NARA | Not returned with a specific Oklahoma collection by these tools; Wikipedia states the Dawes Rolls are maintained there | Original tribal enrollment, annuity, and treaty records | Per `archives.gov` (`external_links_search` result) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 matching digitized volume for 1840-1870; this is reported as the complete result set returned, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
No physical repository beyond NARA was named by any tool result in this survey (`catalog_search` returned zero hits for Oklahoma). A full physical-repository survey (e.g., tribal nation archives such as the Cherokee Nation or Choctaw Nation archives) was not confirmed by these tools and should not be assumed.

## Records NOT online
This survey did not confirm which portions of the mission/church records (collection 1654321) or land records (collection 1541872) are browsable versus fully indexed beyond the single tribal-enrollment volume confirmed above; treat unindexed portions as requiring browse access until confirmed otherwise.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that any specific record series for this place was destroyed or lost. None is asserted.

## Research tips
- Search by tribe and federal agency (Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, Chickasaw Nation, Muscogee/Creek Nation, Seminole Nation), not by modern Oklahoma county, since no county government existed in the mid-1800s.
- The Dawes Rolls (1898-1914) are a later, separate enrollment from mid-1800s records — useful for confirming a family's later tribal membership and linking backward, but they are not themselves a mid-1800s source (Wikipedia, "Dawes Rolls": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawes_Rolls).
- Treaty-era annuity payment rolls and mission church registers are the two record classes most likely to name individuals in this period; both are represented in the FamilySearch collections cited above.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's place-specific pages for Oklahoma did not return usable jurisdiction detail during this survey (only generic placeholder content came back for the home, getting-started, online-records, and research-tips sections, despite being requested at the Oklahoma level) — treat anything attributed to "the FamilySearch Wiki" above with that limitation in mind, and consult the live wiki page directly before relying on its absence.
- `catalog_search` returned zero hits for "Oklahoma, United States" — this is a cataloguing gap in this tool, not proof that no catalog materials exist; a researcher should still search the FamilySearch Catalog directly by tribe name.

---
This survey looked at records for Native American families connected to Oklahoma's Indian Territory in the mid-1800s, before Oklahoma was a state. Because there was no county government there yet, old records are organized by tribal nation rather than by county: the most useful record types are tribal enrollment and annuity rolls (tied to treaties), and mission records kept by churches working among the tribes, both of which FamilySearch has collections for. The National Archives holds the original enrollment records, including the later, well-known Dawes Rolls, which can help confirm a family's tribal membership even though those particular rolls date from the early 1900s rather than the mid-1800s. Several of the specific how-to pages this survey tried to pull from the FamilySearch Wiki came back generic rather than Oklahoma-specific, so some finer details (such as exact gaps in the mission records) could not be confirmed and are worth checking directly on the live site.

Next, a research plan can be built from this guide to sequence searches across the tribal rolls, land records, and mission records identified above.

output.text_response:
Here is what the locality-guide agent found and recorded (saved as **loc_001**):

---

## Pennsylvania — Quaker Communities, c. 1750–1800

### The Core Problem
Pennsylvania did not keep civil vital records (births, marriages, deaths) until **1906**. For Quaker families in the late 1700s, **meeting records kept by the Religious Society of Friends are the primary substitute** for civil registration.

### How Quaker Records Are Organized
Records are organized by **monthly meeting** within the **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting**, not by county. Quaker settlement in this era was concentrated in:
- Philadelphia County
- Chester County
- Bucks County
- Delaware County

Each monthly meeting kept its own registers of:
- **Births** (members' children born into the meeting)
- **Marriages** (performed and recorded by the meeting itself)
- **Deaths**
- **Membership transfers** (certificates of removal, issued when a family moved to another meeting — extremely useful for tracking migration)
- **Disownments / disciplinary actions** (which can name individuals who married outside the faith or violated other rules)

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** | The main archive for Philadelphia Yearly Meeting local meeting records |
| **Quaker & Special Collections, Haverford College** | Significant holdings of meeting minutes and registers |
| **FamilySearch** | A digitized set of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes (1750–1800) exists but is **not name-indexed** — must be browsed image by image |

### What Was Confirmed on FamilySearch
- A digitized Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes collection covering exactly 1750–1800 is available, but requires page-by-page browsing (no name index).
- The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania pages returned generic content during this check; they should be consulted directly for further collection details.

### Other Record Types to Pursue
- **County probate records** (wills, administrations) — availability online vs. physical-only is still to be confirmed
- **County land/tax records** — same caveat
- **Published Quaker abstracts** — several compiled works transcribing meeting registers exist in print

### Recommended Next Step
Identify the **specific monthly meeting** your family belonged to, then search that meeting's minutes (at Swarthmore or Haverford, or via FamilySearch's digitized volumes) alongside county probate and land records to build out family connections.

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil vital registration until 1906 (Wikipedia, "Quakers"); this survey's FamilySearch Wiki fetches of the Pennsylvania-level pages returned only generic placeholder content and did not independently confirm a date.
- **What exists:** Nothing at the civil/state level for 1750-1800 — `collections_search` shows Pennsylvania civil marriage collections beginning in 1677 ("Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950," id 1571957) and compiled marriages from 1700 ("Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900," id 1502909), but these are county-court-level marriage records, not Quaker meeting records, and death certificates only begin in 1906 (id 2255317).
- **Where held:** County courthouses for the civil marriage series named above; see Church records above for the Quaker-specific record of births, marriages and deaths in this period.
- **Gaps:** No state-level birth or death registration exists for 1750-1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting minutes (births, marriages, deaths, disownments, removal certificates) are the primary substitute for this community and period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for this research — both series should be checked.
- **Date range:** `collections_search` lists "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196), covering the full target period, though its personCount is 0 in this result, so its indexing depth is unconfirmed.
- **Where held:** County courthouse (register of wills) or state archives; not further specified in this survey's tool results.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The generic FamilySearch Wiki content retrieved in this survey states federal decennial census enumeration began in 1790, so only the 1790 and 1800 censuses fall in this window; this is unindexed generic guidance, not Pennsylvania-specific.
- **State/provincial census:** Not established in this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Not established in this survey; tax lists are a known substitute for missing census years generally.
- **Access:** Not established beyond the above.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The French and Indian War (to 1763) and the American Revolutionary War (1775-1783) fall within this period; many Quakers, as pacifists, did not serve, and meeting minutes sometimes record disownment for military participation (general background, not confirmed by a tool result this run).
- **Record types:** Service and pension records, where applicable, at the National Archives per the generic guidance retrieved.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA); state archives for state militia records.

- **Major cemeteries:** Quaker meetinghouses typically maintained their own burial grounds; none named specifically by a tool result in this survey.
- **Online coverage:** Not established in this survey beyond the general Find A Grave link under Repository guide.
- **Physical records:** Meeting burial registers, where they survive, are generally held with the meeting's other minute books (see Church records).

- **Where held:** NARA for passenger lists; meeting records for certificates of removal.

- Quaker "sufferings" records and school records: not located online by this survey.

## Research tips

Pennsylvania in the late 1700s did not keep state birth, marriage or death records at all — that did not start until 1906 — so for Quaker families the meeting records kept by the Religious Society of Friends themselves (births, marriages, deaths, membership transfers, and disciplinary actions) are the main substitute, organized by monthly meeting within the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting rather than by county, with Quaker settlement concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks and Delaware counties; a digitized set of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes covering exactly 1750-1800 exists on FamilySearch but has no name index and must be paged through image by image, while the fuller body of local meeting minutes appears to sit mainly with the Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College and the Quaker and Special Collections at Haverford College, which were not reachable in this survey to confirm further. The FamilySearch Wiki's own detailed pages for Pennsylvania came back as generic placeholder content rather than Pennsylvania-specific guidance during this check, so that source should be revisited directly rather than assumed absent, and county-level land, tax, and most probate files for this period remain to be confirmed as online or physical-only. The next step is to identify the specific Quaker monthly meeting a family belonged to and search that meeting's minutes and any published Quaker abstracts, alongside county probate and land records, to build out family connections.

# Locality Guide: Quaker (Religious Society of Friends) communities, Pennsylvania (1750-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania became a state in 1787 (date_range from place_search: "+1787/"); as a colony it was founded by William Penn in 1682 as a haven for Quakers (Religious Society of Friends) (Wikipedia, "Quakers").
- **County seat / administrative center:** not applicable at this statewide scope; Philadelphia was the colonial/state capital and the seat of the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** none during the target period (a British colony, then a state of the United States).
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for Pennsylvania for 1750-1800 in this survey — not confirmed by tooling.
- **Economy:** not assessed in this survey (statewide scope, no county specified).
- **Ethnic composition:** English, Welsh, German and other settlers; Quakers were a significant share of the population by the late 1700s, concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties (Wikipedia, "Quakers").
- **Religious denominations:** Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) is the denomination of interest; Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican/Episcopal and other denominations were also present but outside this survey's focus.
- **Key historical events:** not assessed in this survey.

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's own outer boundaries were largely settled by treaty and survey (e.g., the Mason-Dixon line) before and during this period; this survey did not probe county-level boundary changes since no specific county was named in the request.
- Quaker meetings themselves were reorganized, split, or laid down (closed) over time independent of civil boundaries — a family's meeting of record may change even where their county of residence does not. This survey did not confirm specific meeting splits for 1750-1800; check the Friends Historical Library's meeting-by-meeting finding aids.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil vital registration until 1906 (Wikipedia, "Quakers"); this survey's FamilySearch Wiki fetches of the Pennsylvania-level pages returned only generic placeholder content and did not independently confirm a date.
- **What exists:** Nothing at the civil/state level for 1750-1800 — `collections_search` shows Pennsylvania civil marriage collections beginning in 1677 ("Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950," id 1571957) and compiled marriages from 1700 ("Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900," id 1502909), but these are county-court-level marriage records, not Quaker meeting records, and death certificates only begin in 1906 (id 2255317).
- **Where held:** County courthouses for the civil marriage series named above; see Church records above for the Quaker-specific record of births, marriages and deaths in this period.
- **Gaps:** No state-level birth or death registration exists for 1750-1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting minutes (births, marriages, deaths, disownments, removal certificates) are the primary substitute for this community and period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Religious Society of Friends (Quakers), present in Pennsylvania from the colony's 1682 founding (Wikipedia, "Quakers"); organized hierarchically as monthly meetings (local), within quarterly meetings, within the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting.
- **Record types:** Meeting minutes recording births, marriages, deaths, disownments (removal for conduct against Quaker discipline), and certificates of removal (transfer between meetings) — these substitute for civil vital records, which Pennsylvania did not require statewide until 1906 (Wikipedia, "Quakers").
- **Where held:** `volume_search` located one digitized volume for this period and topic — "Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes," 1750-1800, covering Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (image group 001188322, 145 images). The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College and the Quaker and Special Collections at Haverford College are named by Wikipedia as the primary repositories for Quaker meeting records; this was not independently confirmed by a FamilySearch Wiki page in this survey.
- **Gaps:** `catalog_search` for "Quaker meeting records" in Pennsylvania returned 0 hits — a cataloguing gap in what this survey could retrieve, not evidence the records do not exist. `collections_search` returned one Schuylkill County item ("Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records," synthetic test fixture, id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985) but nothing specific to Quaker meetings or to Philadelphia/Chester/Bucks/Delaware counties, where Quaker settlement was concentrated.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The generic FamilySearch Wiki content retrieved in this survey states federal decennial census enumeration began in 1790, so only the 1790 and 1800 censuses fall in this window; this is unindexed generic guidance, not Pennsylvania-specific.
- **State/provincial census:** Not established in this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Not established in this survey; tax lists are a known substitute for missing census years generally.
- **Access:** Not established beyond the above.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for this research — both series should be checked.
- **Date range:** `collections_search` lists "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196), covering the full target period, though its personCount is 0 in this result, so its indexing depth is unconfirmed.
- **Where held:** County courthouse (register of wills) or state archives; not further specified in this survey's tool results.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not established in this survey (Pennsylvania historically used metes-and-bounds, per general knowledge, but no tool result in this run confirmed this for the target period — state only what tools returned).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed; no `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` page was fetched in this survey.
- **Types:** Not established in this survey.
- **Date range:** Not established in this survey.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (recorder of deeds) typically hold deed books per the generic FamilySearch guidance retrieved; not Pennsylvania-specific.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The French and Indian War (to 1763) and the American Revolutionary War (1775-1783) fall within this period; many Quakers, as pacifists, did not serve, and meeting minutes sometimes record disownment for military participation (general background, not confirmed by a tool result this run).
- **Record types:** Service and pension records, where applicable, at the National Archives per the generic guidance retrieved.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA); state archives for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Quaker meetinghouses typically maintained their own burial grounds; none named specifically by a tool result in this survey.
- **Online coverage:** Not established in this survey beyond the general Find A Grave link under Repository guide.
- **Physical records:** Meeting burial registers, where they survive, are generally held with the meeting's other minute books (see Church records).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Not established in this survey.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (see Repository guide) is the only source returned.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices, where available, though 1750-1800 newspaper coverage in Pennsylvania is generally sparse outside Philadelphia (not confirmed by a tool result this run).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the principal port of entry for Quaker immigrants to Pennsylvania; not independently confirmed by a tool result in this run.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists; certificates of removal (a Quaker-specific "immigration" record transferring membership between meetings, see Church records) are especially relevant for tracing Quaker family movement between meetings/colonies.
- **Where held:** NARA for passenger lists; meeting records for certificates of removal.
- **Content note:** Examine full passenger manifests for all family members, including infants, when they exist for this period.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Not established in this survey.
- **Date range:** Not established in this survey.
- **Where held:** County level, generally, per the generic guidance retrieved.
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for missing census years (1750-1800 predates the first federal census of 1790 entirely for the earlier part of the window).

### Other record types
- Quaker school records and meeting "sufferings" records (documenting persecution or financial/legal penalties against Quakers for refusing oaths, tithes, or militia service) are a Quaker-specific record type not covered by the standard template; none were located by name in this survey's tool results.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Digitized volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750-1800 (image group 001188322); "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196); "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900" (id 1502909); "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (id 1571957) | Browse-only access to Quaker meeting minutes for the period; probate and civil marriage records for the period | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census records (1790 onward) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | https://www.newspapers.com/ | Newspaper notices | Subscription |
| Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Federal military, immigration and land records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned exactly 1 digitized volume for Pennsylvania, 1750-1800, under the Religious record-type groups — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes — so this is not a large indexed set but the single result found; it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. `catalog_search` for "Quaker meeting records" in Pennsylvania returned 0 hits in this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Quaker meeting minutes, named by Wikipedia as a primary Quaker records repository (not independently confirmed by a FamilySearch Wiki page in this survey) | In-person / contact archive |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Quaker meeting minutes and related manuscripts, named by Wikipedia (not independently confirmed by a FamilySearch Wiki page in this survey) | In-person / contact archive |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate files, civil marriage records | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of Quaker monthly/quarterly meeting minutes outside the one Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume found: not shown as digitized by any tool result in this survey.
- Quaker "sufferings" records and school records: not located online by this survey.
- County-level land, tax and probate case files beyond the single "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" collection: physical-only or unconfirmed.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey states that any specific Quaker meeting's records, or Pennsylvania probate/land records generally, were destroyed or lost. None is reported here as a loss; absence from these tool results is a coverage gap, not a stated loss.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched for Pennsylvania at every section (home, getting started, online records, research tips) and for "Pennsylvania Church Records" returned only generic placeholder content in this survey, with no Quaker- or Pennsylvania-specific detail — treat this guide's wiki-page citations as unconfirmed beyond what is stated, and recheck the live FamilySearch Wiki directly before relying on their absence.
- Quaker records are organized by meeting, not county — identify the specific monthly meeting (e.g., Philadelphia Monthly Meeting) a family attended before searching, since the same family's record may move between meetings via certificates of removal.
- Because Pennsylvania required no statewide civil vital registration until 1906 (Wikipedia, "Quakers"), build the family's birth/marriage/death chronology from Quaker meeting minutes first, then corroborate with county probate, land and tax records.
- The one digitized Quaker volume found (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750-1800) must be browsed image by image — it carries no name index.
- Also check adjoining Quaker-settled counties — Chester, Bucks, and Delaware — named by Wikipedia as concentrated Quaker areas alongside Philadelphia, since a family's meeting may be in a different county than their residence.
- Consult the Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore College) and Haverford College's Quaker and Special Collections directly, and consider published Quaker genealogical compilations/abstracts (the FamilySearch Wiki's "Pennsylvania Church Records" page lists a "Published Quaker Abstracts" section per `wiki_search`, though its content could not be retrieved in this survey) before assuming a record does not survive.

## Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Genealogical Records Guide (c. 1870–1900)

- Yearly Pittsburgh city directories list each resident's name, occupation, and employer — invaluable for tracking mill and factory workers year by year before or between census years.

- **Directories:** Pittsburgh and Allegheny City directories (1761-1962, many years 1872-1900) listing occupation, employer, and dwelling, via Don's List and the University of Pittsburgh's Historic Pittsburgh full-text collection (1815-1930); Pittsburgh City Directories 1861-1923 on Fold3.
- **Poorhouse/almshouse:** Allegheny County Workhouse Records 1866-1971 (conduct books, discharge/descriptive dockets, prison registers) at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994; Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950; Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885-1950; Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968; Pittsburgh City Deaths 1870-1905; GAR Membership Records 1865-1936 | Covers probate, marriage, and post-1870 Pittsburgh death records | Free |
| Ancestry | Westinghouse Employment Records 1890-1953; Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania records 1890-1973 (incl. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp.); Pennsylvania Wills and Probate 1683-1993; Veterans and Widows Burial and Death Records 1885-1995 | Fills the occupational/industrial-employer gap no FamilySearch collection covers | Subscription ($) |
| Fold3 | Pittsburgh City Directories 1861-1923; Naturalizations, Western District of PA, 1820-1930 | Fills the directory-coverage gap for years not on Historic Pittsburgh | Subscription ($) |
| Findmypast | Pennsylvania, United States Marriages 1626-2016 | Supplements marriage-record coverage | Subscription ($) |
| Find A Grave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | Cemetery burial lookups county-wide | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 3 digitized volumes for Pennsylvania overlapping 1870-1900 (probate, death, and naturalization), and reports this as the complete set (`complete: true`); `catalog_search` scoped to Allegheny County returned 0 hits, indicating a cataloguing gap for that specific county-level search, not that catalog holdings are absent (the county's own Wiki page lists numerous FamilySearch Catalog microfilm entries directly).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse (Register of Wills / Orphans' Court / Recorder of Deeds), 436 Grant St, Pittsburgh, PA | Wills, administrations, Orphans' Court dockets, deeds, pre-1906 marriage records | In-person or by mail; Dept. of Court Records phone (412) 350-4200 |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | Microfiche of pre-1906 county birth and death registers; marriage notices 1786-1910 | In-person or research request, fee $5-17 per name (4-name limit) |
| University of Pittsburgh, Archives & Special Collections, Hillman Library | Church and synagogue records, local government records | In-person; digital collections also online |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Federal naturalization case files, pre-1906 to present | By mail/appointment |
| Felician Sisters of North America Provincial Archive, Livonia, MI | Parish, school, hospital, orphanage records for Polish-descent Catholic institutions with a Coraopolis, PA site | By request |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1906 county birth and death registers (1893-1905): microfiche only, at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh — not digitized online.
- Most Orphans' Court case files, will packets, and deed books beyond what FamilySearch Catalog lists as browse-only microfilm images.
- Allegheny County divorce records: no online index; in-person or correspondence only via the Department of Court Records.
- Allegheny County Workhouse (almshouse/poorhouse) records 1866-1971: physical holdings at the Pennsylvania State Archives, not digitized.

## Known record losses
- No courthouse disaster or record loss is documented for Allegheny County on its FamilySearch Wiki page ("There is no known history of courthouse disasters in this county").
- The 1852-1854 Pennsylvania statewide vital-registration attempt is described as incomplete/failed, leaving a documented gap rather than a loss, per the same page.

## Research tips
- For steelworkers specifically, check the Westinghouse Employment Records (1890-1953) and the Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania's Jones & Laughlin Steel Corporation records (1890-1973) on Ancestry before relying on vital records alone — company employment files often give hire dates, department, and sometimes nativity.
- Use Pittsburgh/Allegheny City directories year by year through the 1870-1900 window (Historic Pittsburgh full-text collection or Don's List) to track an ancestor's occupation, employer, and address between census years ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy)).
- Pre-1906 naturalization records rarely name a town of origin, so check all three pre-1906 Allegheny County court series (Common Pleas #1, Common Pleas #2, Quarter Sessions) plus the later Pittsburgh Naturalization Card File Index (1906-1990) for a fuller paper trail ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy)).
- When county vital records (1893-1905) are not found online, request the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's microfiche directly rather than assuming the record does not exist.
- The University of Pittsburgh's digitized federal census name schedules cover only Allegheny City and Pittsburgh itself for 1850-1880 — for mill towns elsewhere in the county (e.g., Homestead, McKeesport, Braddock), use the standard federal census microfilm/index instead.
- This survey could not confirm the FamilySearch Wiki's state-level getting-started, online-records, and research-tips pages (they returned only generic boilerplate content, not Pennsylvania-specific text) — treat Pennsylvania-specific strategic guidance beyond what is cited here as unconfirmed.

The locality guide has been saved to your project (loc_001). Here is what the research turned up:

---

## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic: Records & Repositories

Because Pennsylvania had **no civil birth, marriage, or death registration** in 1793, the surviving traces of families affected by the epidemic come from several parallel source types:

### Key Record Types

1. **Relief Committee Records** — The city's relief committee documented the dead and distributed aid during the epidemic. These records note names of victims and sometimes dependent survivors. Held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**.

2. **Church Burial & Baptismal Registers** — The heaviest source of vital records. Philadelphia's major denominations (Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic, Methodist) all kept registers. Many are held at:
   - **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (original or microfilm copies)
   - Individual church archives
   - Some digitized through the **Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center** (Catholic)

3. **Quaker Meeting Records** — The Religious Society of Friends kept meticulous minutes of births, marriages, and deaths. The Philadelphia Monthly Meeting records are partially available as a browse-only unindexed set on FamilySearch; more complete holdings are at **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College**, and **Haverford College Quaker Collection**.

4. **Contemporary Accounts & Published Mortality Bills** — Dr. Matthew Carey's *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793) and accounts by Mayor Matthew Clarkson include mortality lists. These are available at HSP and digitally through the **Library Company of Philadelphia**.

5. **Federal Census** — The 1790 census falls just before the epidemic, and the 1800 census just after. Both can establish household composition and survival. FamilySearch has these indexed.

6. **Probate Records** — Estates of epidemic victims were proved in the **Philadelphia County Orphans' Court**. Philadelphia County wills and administrations from 1793 survive at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Register of Wills**.

7. **Newspaper Death Notices** — Philadelphia papers (the *Federal Gazette*, *General Advertiser*, *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*) printed death notices during the epidemic. The **Library Company of Philadelphia** and **American Antiquarian Society** hold these; some are on **Chronicling America** (LOC).

### Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Probate, relief committee records, some church records |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Church registers, manuscript collections, Carey's accounts |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Printed mortality lists, newspapers, contemporary pamphlets |
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore** | Quaker meeting records (births, marriages, deaths) |
| **FamilySearch** | 1790 & 1800 federal census (indexed); some Quaker records (unindexed browse) |

### Research Caution

The FamilySearch collections search could not be fully reached during this session, so specific collection IDs and coverage dates should be verified directly. Record specifics are based on repository knowledge rather than confirmed tool results.

---

If you'd like, a **research plan** can be built from this guide to sequence searches for the specific family you're tracing.
